oneLiner: Completes the cloning pipeline (transform → select → screen → confirm → express → purify) and surveys applications of genetic engineering in medicine, agriculture, industry and environment, plus biosafety and ethics.

sections.heading: Transformation, selection, screening, confirmation
points: Pipeline: isolate gene → insert into vector → transform host → select → screen → confirm → express → purify.
Transformation: recombinant plasmid into competent cells by heat shock (~42°C) or electroporation (high-voltage pulse); both open temporary membrane pores.
Cells recover before plating on selective (antibiotic) medium; plasmid needs origin of replication + selectable marker (e.g., AmpR).
Selection = survival on antibiotic → cell has plasmid; does NOT prove insert present.
Screening identifies likely recombinants (white colonies in the shown scheme); still needs confirmation.
Confirmation: colony PCR (insert from colony), restriction digestion (fragment pattern), DNA sequencing (exact sequence + insert orientation).

sections.heading: Expression of recombinant protein
points: Inserted gene transcribed to mRNA, translated to protein inside host.
Promoter controls when, where and how strongly a gene is transcribed; expression vector needs promoter + translation-control elements.
Inducible systems: lac, T7, ara; IPTG induces lac-based expression; T7 = high-expression E. coli system.
Induction separates cell growth from strong protein production.
Workflow order: transform → grow culture → induce → harvest → lyse → purify.

sections.heading: Purification and analysis (Ni-NTA, SDS-PAGE)
points: His-tag (short histidine stretch) binds Ni²⁺ on Ni-NTA affinity resin.
Wash with LOW imidazole removes weak/nonspecific binders; HIGH imidazole competes with His-tag → elutes target.
SDS denatures proteins and gives similar charge-to-mass ratio → separation mainly by molecular weight (kDa).
Smaller proteins migrate farther (lower on gel); strong band at expected size supports expression and purity.

sections.heading: Medical applications
points: Recombinant human insulin: human gene cloned, expressed in E. coli, purified and processed — classic recombinant protein.
hGH → growth hormone deficiency; EPO → RBC production in anemia; interferons → antiviral, some cancers; Factor VIII → hemophilia A, Factor IX → hemophilia B.
Recombinant vaccines (subunit, VLP, recombinant vector) avoid whole infectious pathogen; hepatitis B vaccine = HBsAg made in yeast, non-infectious, approved 1986.
Monoclonal antibodies bind one specific target (e.g., HER2, RSV); made in mammalian cells for proper folding/processing.
Gene therapy strategies: replacement, addition, silencing (siRNA), editing (CRISPR).
Examples: SMA = in vivo gene addition; sickle cell = ex vivo editing of BCL11A enhancer → fetal hemoglobin restored; CAR-T = engineered T cells.

sections.heading: Agricultural applications
points: Targets: biotic stress (pests, pathogens), abiotic stress (drought, salinity, heat, cold), nutrition, yield, shelf life.
Bt crops express Cry insecticidal proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis against specific pests; reduce insecticide use.
Bt concerns: insect resistance (needs resistance management), non-target effects, gene flow, biosafety.
Golden Rice: genes activate carotenoid pathway → β-carotene (provitamin A) in endosperm; biofortification vs vitamin A deficiency.
Other traits: herbicide tolerance, disease resistance, delayed ripening (shelf life); edible vaccine banana (viral proteins), scorpion-gene cabbage (deters insects).
High US adoption (2010) of GM soybean, cotton, corn, sugar beet; Bt corn protein toxic to certain insects, stated not poisonous to humans.

sections.heading: Industrial, environmental and animal applications
points: Industry: chymosin (cheese), lactase (lactose breakdown), amylase, protease, lipase, amino acids, vitamins, ethanol, bioplastics; advantages: yield, consistency, scalability, lower cost.
Environment: bioremediation, wastewater treatment, biosensors, sustainable bioprocesses.
Bacteria are common GMOs (easy to manipulate): cyanobacteria → polyethylene/butanol; E. coli → diesel.
Knockout mouse (hair-growth gene → hairless) removes function; GFP mice/GloFish add expression; fluorescence/BLI for protein tracking and disease detection.
Fast-growing salmon: genes from two other fish → continual growth hormone; modified methane-producing gut bacteria → ~25% less cattle methane.
Transgenic goats with spider genes produce spider-silk protein in milk (animal as production host).

sections.heading: Concerns, biosafety, ethics and future
points: GMO concerns: food safety, environmental/wildlife harm, pesticide/herbicide use, farmer health, seed/pollen drift, herbicide-resistant weeds (superweeds); varied labeling/bans.
Biosafety: unintended/off-target changes, lab and release risks, gene flow, ecosystem and non-target effects.
Ethics: germline editing (heritable), consent, fairness, misuse; regulation = safety testing, approval, post-release monitoring.
Challenges: delivery, cost, regulation, uncertain long-term effects.
Future: base editing (no standard double-strand break), prime editing, improved CRISPR, personalized medicine, synthetic biology, therapeutic cells, greener fuels/materials.

mustRemember: Vector essentials: ori + selectable marker + MCS; expression vector adds promoter + translation controls
Use cDNA (no introns) to express human gene in E. coli
Heat shock ≈ 42°C; electroporation = high-voltage pulse
IPTG induces lac system; lac, T7, ara = inducible systems
His-tag binds Ni²⁺ (Ni-NTA); low imidazole wash, high imidazole elute
SDS-PAGE separates by size; small proteins run lower
Sequencing confirms identity AND orientation of insert
Factor VIII → hemophilia A; Factor IX → hemophilia B; EPO → anemia
Hep B vaccine = recombinant HBsAg in yeast, approved 1986
Sickle cell: ex vivo edit of BCL11A enhancer → fetal Hb ↑; SMA: in vivo gene addition
Bt = Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxin; Golden Rice = β-carotene in endosperm
Cattle methane ↓ ~25%; salmon genes from two other fish; goat milk spider silk
Chymosin → cheese; lactase → lactose breakdown

distinguish.difference: Selection keeps cells carrying the marker plasmid; screening identifies colonies likely carrying the insert.
Screening flags likely recombinants; confirmation (colony PCR, digest, sequencing) tests the insert directly.
Cloning vector only propagates DNA; expression vector also has promoter/translation elements for protein production.
Genomic DNA has introns bacteria cannot splice; cDNA from processed mRNA lacks introns.
Low imidazole washes off contaminants; high imidazole competes off and elutes the His-tagged protein.
Bt = insect resistance via Cry toxin; Golden Rice = provitamin A (β-carotene) biofortification.

distinguish.pair: In vivo vs Ex vivo gene therapy
distinguish.difference: In vivo modifies cells inside the body (SMA); ex vivo modifies cells outside then returns them (sickle cell).
Biotic = living agents (pests, pathogens); abiotic = drought, salinity, heat, cold.

traps: Antibiotic survival proves the marker plasmid is present, not the desired insert.
A cloning vector is not automatically an expression vector.
Low imidazole washes; high imidazole elutes — don't swap them.
Bt and Golden Rice solve different problems (insects vs vitamin A).
Monoclonal antibodies need mammalian cells, not E. coli, for proper folding/processing.
Germline editing is heritable; somatic gene therapy is not passed on.

oneLiner: Molecular motors convert chemical energy (ATP/GTP hydrolysis) into directed motion via nucleotide-driven conformational cycles; actin–myosin is the key example, and optical tweezers measure single-myosin steps (~11 nm) and forces (~3 pN).

sections.heading: Energy and nonequilibrium basis
points: Conventional motor: electrical → mechanical energy; biological motor: chemical → mechanical energy (or other directed work).
Many required cellular reactions are unfavorable; cells need continuous energy input.
Life is nonequilibrium: ordered structures, concentration and charge gradients (e.g., proton pumps keep lysosomes acidic).
Molecular machines transduce one store of free energy into another.

sections.heading: Why molecular motors are different
points: Nanometer scale, in water, low Reynolds number (viscous forces dominate inertia).
Brownian motion makes environment stochastic.
Rely on noncovalent interactions and internal protein dynamics, not rigid parts; sensitive to temperature and pH.

sections.heading: Fundamental principles: ATP/GTP and conformational change
points: Molecular motor = macromolecular complex converting energy into directed motion/function.
Principle 1: energy from ATP or GTP; ATP → ADP + Pi, standard ΔG ≈ −7.3 kcal/mol; ATPases hydrolyze, ATP synthase makes ATP.
Principle 2: ATP binding, hydrolysis, Pi release and ADP→ATP exchange switch protein between conformations (State A/B).
ATP/GTP-bound = active; ADP/GDP-bound = inactive; only selected regions change shape.
Repeated mechanochemical cycle converts chemical events into movement.

sections.heading: Motor categories and cytoskeleton
points: Four categories: polymerization, cytoskeletal (actin–myosin), rotary (bacterial flagella), nucleic-acid motors.
Cytoskeleton: dynamic 3D network for shape, motility, cytokinesis, transport, division, organelle organization.
Three filament systems: actin microfilaments, intermediate filaments, tubulin microtubules.
Myosin moves on actin tracks (fluorescence: myosin-II green, actin blue).

sections.heading: Actin structure and polymerization
points: G-actin = globular soluble monomer; F-actin = filamentous polymer (right-handed, two-stranded helix, polar).
Assembly: slow nucleation (unstable seed) → elongation at both ends, faster at plus (barbed) than minus (pointed) end.
Actin binds ATP and is an ATPase; polymerization promotes hydrolysis; ATP-actin adds more readily, ADP-actin dissociates more readily.
Steady state: constant F-actin mass; treadmilling = plus-end addition + minus-end loss.
Critical concentration separates net polymerization from net depolymerization; actin-binding proteins and Ca²⁺ regulate assembly.

sections.heading: Muscle: sarcomere and myosin
points: Striations reflect ordered repeating organization of muscle fibers.
Sarcomere = Z line to Z line; thin actin filaments anchored at Z lines; thick myosin filaments centered at M line; overlap gives banding.
Myosin: two heavy chains + essential and regulatory light chains.
Head (motor domain) binds actin and ATP; neck carries light chains; tail = dimeric coiled-coil (dimerization, cargo/filament).
Cross-bridge cycle: attach → force generation → detach → reset, controlled by ATP.

sections.heading: Optical tweezers physics
points: Arthur Ashkin: tightly focused laser traps a dielectric particle in 3D.
Light carries momentum; bead refracts/reflects light → equal and opposite momentum change = force.
Gaussian beam brightest at center; scattering force ∝ intensity, along beam propagation.
Gradient force pulls bead toward high-intensity center = restoring force.
Near center trap acts as spring: F = −kx (k = trap stiffness); displacement → force.

sections.heading: Single-myosin measurements and applications
points: Dual-beam trap: actin held taut (~2 pN) between two trapped beads, lowered onto pedestal bead sparsely coated with myosin (isolates single motors).
Quadrant photodiode tracks bead position; bead displacement reports stroke size, attachment lifetime, force.
Working stroke ≈ 11 nm (cluster ~10–13 nm), similar at low and high ATP; measured along actin.
Single myosin force ~2–5 pN, peak near 3 pN.
Biohybrids: bacteria-powered, light-controlled 3D micromotors; bacterial flagellar motor = rotary motor turning helical flagellum.

mustRemember: ATP → ADP + Pi, ΔG°′ ≈ −7.3 kcal/mol
Cycle: bind → hydrolyze → release → exchange
Four motor classes: polymerization, cytoskeletal, rotary, nucleic-acid
Microfilament = actin; microtubule = tubulin; + intermediate filaments
Plus (barbed) end grows faster than minus (pointed) end
Treadmilling: add at plus, lose at minus, constant mass
Sarcomere: Z line to Z line; M line at centre; actin thin, myosin thick
Myosin: head (actin + ATP), neck (light chains), tail (coiled-coil dimer)
Hooke's law F = −kx for optical trap
pN = 10⁻¹² N; nm = 10⁻⁹ m
Myosin step ≈ 11 nm; force peak ≈ 3 pN (2–5 pN); actin tension ≈ 2 pN
Arthur Ashkin = optical tweezers; quadrant photodiode detects bead position

distinguish.difference: G-actin is the globular monomer; F-actin is the polar helical filament polymer of the same protein.
Plus end adds subunits faster; minus end grows slower and loses subunits in treadmilling.
ATP-actin preferentially adds to filaments; ADP-actin dissociates more readily.
Scattering pushes along beam direction; gradient pulls toward bright beam center (restoring).
Macroscopic use rigid parts and inertia; molecular work at low Reynolds number, Brownian, noncovalent, protein dynamics.
Z line bounds the sarcomere and anchors thin actin; M line is the center with thick myosin.
ATP/GTP-bound = active; ADP/GDP-bound = inactive.

traps: ATP is not just stored fuel: binding, hydrolysis, release and exchange each change motor conformation.
G-actin and F-actin are two assembly states of one protein, not different proteins.
Scattering force follows the beam; gradient force is the centering/restoring force.
Optical tweezers read bead displacement; force is inferred via F = −kx.
Steady state ≠ inactive: subunits still flux through via treadmilling.
Myosin step size (~11 nm) does not change with ATP concentration in the shown traces.

oneLiner: Cells sense signals via receptors, process them through cascades with amplification and integration, and respond; the GPCR–G protein–cAMP–PKA pathway is the core example, with GTP hydrolysis, GRK and arrestin providing shutoff.

sections.heading: Signaling as a control system
points: Sensor → information processing → response.
Properties: specificity, cascade, amplification, feedback, integration.
Cells receive multiple signals simultaneously and integrate them into one response.
Pathways form networks: convergence (different receptors → shared component) and divergence (one signal → multiple outputs).
Only target cells with suitable receptor and state respond; responses rapid or slow.

sections.heading: Signal chemistry and modes of signaling
points: Chemical types: amino-acid derivatives, gases (NO, CO), steroids (from cholesterol), peptides/proteins, surface-bound molecules.
Autocrine: cell responds to its own signal.
Paracrine: short-range to nearby cells (PDGF in wound repair).
Juxtacrine: direct contact between surface molecules (Delta).
Endocrine: via bloodstream to distant targets (insulin from pancreatic β cells).

sections.heading: Examples of hormones and local mediators
points: Adrenal: epinephrine, cortisol (steroid); pancreas α cells: glucagon (fuel mobilization); β cells: insulin (glucose uptake); thyroid: thyroxine.
Steroids: cortisol, estradiol, testosterone.
EGF, PDGF → proliferation; NGF supports neurons; TGF-β inhibits proliferation.
Histamine (mast cells) → vessel dilation and leakiness in inflammation; GABA = inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter.

sections.heading: Intracellular (nuclear) receptor signaling
points: Lipid-soluble steroids cross plasma membrane, bind intracellular receptors.
Cortisol → glucocorticoid receptor → complex to nucleus → binds DNA → alters transcription.
Response requires new protein synthesis (slower).
Non-crossing signals use cell-surface receptors and intracellular relays.

sections.heading: Cell-surface receptors and GPCR structure
points: Three classes: GPCRs, receptor tyrosine kinases (phosphorylate tyrosines), ligand-gated ion channels.
GPCR = seven transmembrane α-helix bundle; ligand binding changes conformation transmitted to intracellular side.
Activates heterotrimeric G protein (α, β, γ) → effector (e.g., adenylyl cyclase).
GPCR ligands: epinephrine, serotonin, light (rhodopsin), odorants, fMet peptides, acetylcholine; specificity from receptor, G protein, effector, cell context.

sections.heading: GPCR–G protein cycle and cAMP
points: Ligand binds GPCR → GDP released, GTP binds Gα → Gα-GTP activates effector → adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP from ATP.
Gα hydrolyzes GTP (GTPase) → off → reassociates with βγ (trimer reforms).
Amplification: one active receptor activates multiple G proteins; diffusible cAMP reaches many targets.
cAMP = cyclic AMP: phosphate forms cyclic linkage with ribose; second messenger (ligand = first messenger), e.g., serotonin in Aplysia neuron.
Phosphodiesterase converts cAMP → AMP, terminating signal.

sections.heading: Liver cAMP cascade
points: Glucagon/epinephrine → GPCR → G protein → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA).
PKA activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase → glycogen breakdown, glucose release.
Nuclear branch: PKA phosphorylates/activates CREB → altered gene transcription.

sections.heading: Attenuation / desensitization
points: GRK phosphorylates the active GPCR → high-affinity arrestin site.
Arrestin and G protein compete for same cytoplasmic receptor cavity → arrestin blocks further G-protein activation.
Arrestin can promote receptor internalization (coated pit → vesicle → recycling).
Desensitization = reduced signaling despite continued ligand presence.

mustRemember: Sensor → processing → response; cascade, amplification, feedback, integration, specificity
Autocrine (self), paracrine (local, PDGF), juxtacrine (contact, Delta), endocrine (blood, insulin)
Gaseous signals: NO, CO; steroids derived from cholesterol
Glucagon = pancreatic α cells; insulin = β cells; epinephrine, cortisol = adrenal; thyroxine = thyroid
TGF-β inhibits proliferation; EGF/PDGF stimulate; GABA inhibitory CNS
Cortisol → intracellular glucocorticoid receptor → transcription
Three surface receptor classes: GPCR, RTK, ion channel
GPCR = 7 transmembrane helices; G protein = αβγ heterotrimer
Gα: GDP→GTP exchange = ON; GTP hydrolysis = OFF
Adenylyl cyclase: ATP → cAMP; phosphodiesterase: cAMP → AMP
cAMP → PKA → glycogen phosphorylase ↑, glycogen synthase ↓, CREB ↑
GRK phosphorylates receptor → arrestin binds → blocks G protein, internalization
Rhodopsin = light-detecting GPCR

distinguish.difference: Paracrine acts locally on nearby cells; endocrine travels in blood to distant targets.
Autocrine: cell responds to its own secreted signal; juxtacrine: requires direct cell-surface contact.
Lipid-soluble steroids bind intracellular receptors and change transcription; others bind surface receptors and use relays.
GPCR is the seven-transmembrane receptor; G protein is the separate trimeric GTP-binding switch.
First = extracellular ligand binding receptor; second = intracellular small molecule like cAMP.
Both adenine + ribose + phosphate; in cAMP the phosphate forms a cyclic bond with ribose.
Amplification: one receptor → many G proteins, cAMP; attenuation: GTP hydrolysis, GRK, arrestin, PDE.
Convergence: many inputs meet at a shared component; divergence: one input branches to several outputs.

traps: Signaling types are classified by route and distance, not chemical identity of the messenger.
Endocrine = bloodstream to distant targets; paracrine = short-range local.
cAMP amplifies; GTP hydrolysis plus GRK and arrestin shut off — don't confuse activation with attenuation.
Arrestin binds only the active phosphorylated receptor, competing with the G protein for the same site.
Steroid (cortisol) responses need new protein synthesis via transcription, not a second messenger.
